ghs.en: On the way home,
Nanaka: "Heeey!"
Nanaka was right next to me.

Taichi: "Ah, Nanaka..."
Nanaka: "In spiriiits?"
ghs.assessment: お元気 is the greeting 'How are you?' Stretching the vowel does not make the bare prepositional fragment functional English.

highlights.text: In spiriiits?

rows.jp: 「そんなことより、あの祠って―――」

ghs.en: Taichi: "More importantly, that hokora---"
ghs.assessment: 祠 is a small shrine. The English leaves the common noun as an unexplained romanized Japanese word instead of translating it.

highlights.text: hokora

ghs.en: I was embraced.
Taichi: "N'uguh?"

rows.jp: 「楽しいって、言えるなら、いいじゃん」
rows.en: “If you can say you’re having fun, that’s good enough.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "You said fun, and if you can say that, 's all right."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that it is good if he can call the experience fun. The English first asserts that he already said the isolated word 'fun,' contradicting the following denial.

highlights.text: You said fun, and if you can say that

ghs.en: Taichi: "No, I didn't say that."

rows.jp: つうか会話に脈絡ないんですけど。
rows.en: Also, this conversation has no continuity.

ghs.en: There is no chain of logical connection going through this conversation, however,
ghs.assessment: The Japanese colloquially says that the conversation has no logical continuity. The English expands this into an awkward literal chain running through it.

highlights.text: no chain of logical connection going through this conversation

rows.jp: なんなんだこの唐突感動イベントは……。
rows.en: What is this sudden tearjerker event...?

ghs.en: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event...
ghs.assessment: The Japanese asks what this sudden touching scene is. The English question lacks a grammatical predicate and gratuitously capitalizes its descriptive phrase.

highlights.text: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event

rows.jp: しかし、それはそれとして。

ghs.en: Anyway, be that as it may.

rows.jp: あいまいな胸の柔らかさ。
rows.en: The indistinct softness of her chest.

ghs.en: The ambiguous softness of a breast.
The scent of a girl.

rows.jp: 不思議と、猥雑なものは感じない。
rows.en: Strangely, it didn’t feel the least bit obscene.

ghs.en: Inexplicably, I feel nothing out of order.
ghs.assessment: 猥雑 specifically means something lewd, vulgar, or sexually sordid. The English erases that dimension and substitutes the vague idea of disorder.

highlights.text: nothing out of order

rows.jp: 抱かれた時の感覚が、曜子ちゃんとは違った。
rows.en: Being held by her felt different from being held by Yoko.

ghs.en: The feeling at the moment of embrace was so different from Youko-chan's.

rows.jp: 「その言葉は、嬉しいんだ。すごく」
rows.en: “Hearing you say that makes me happy. So happy.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Those words... they make me happy. Really."
Taichi: "But I didn't say anything..."

rows.jp: 「強くならないと生きる資格がないわけじゃないから」
rows.en: “You don’t have to become strong to deserve to live.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Because never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that one need not become strong in order to deserve to live. 'Never becoming strong' adds permanent future failure and the nominal construction is an awkward calque.

highlights.text: never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living

rows.en: “You haven't heard a word I've said.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Listen to what you're being told!"
ghs.assessment: 聞いちゃいねぇ means that Taichi was not listening or did not ask for the speech. The English instead orders Nanaka to listen.

highlights.text: Listen to what you're being told!

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Remaining weak is... still fine."
Taichi: "You listening or not!"

rows.jp: わけがわからなかった。
rows.en: I had no idea what was going on.

ghs.en: I didn't understand any of this.

rows.jp: 「胸の感触はすごくよかった」

ghs.en: Taichi: "I'm really glad to have experienced the tactile feeling of your chest."
Nanaka: "...too honest."

rows.jp: 「ただわけはわからなかった」
rows.en: “I just had no idea what was going on.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "It's just that I didn't get this at all."
Nanaka: "Sorry, I mistook you, 's all."
ghs.assessment: Nanaka says that she was mistaken or got something wrong. 'Mistook you' specifically claims that she confused Taichi's identity with another person's.

highlights.text: I mistook you

ghs.en: Taichi: "For what?"
ghs.assessment: Taichi asks what she mistook him for. 'For what?' instead asks the purpose or reason.

highlights.text: For what?

ghs.en: Nanaka scratched her head.
Nanaka: "A different one."

rows.jp: 「理解できるように説明して」

ghs.en: Taichi: "Explain in ways I can understand."
ghs.assessment: The line asks for a single intelligible manner of explanation; the English plural produces a malformed collocation.

highlights.text: in ways I can understand

rows.jp: 「キミってアンテナ設営の方、着手したみたいだけど、進捗はどう？」
rows.en: “Seems like you've started setting up the antenna. How's it going?”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he seems to have begun the antenna installation and asks how it is progressing. The English adds 'helping,' uses a malformed 'setting out on ... construction,' and omits the article before 'progress.'

highlights.text: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"

ghs.en: Taichi: "Listen here."
Nanaka: "W'at?"

rows.jp: 「わかるように話そう。まず……まずだ」
rows.en: “Let's try this in words I can understand. First... first of all.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Let's talk so that I can understand. First... first up is..."
Nanaka: "First?"

rows.jp: 「そうだな、いろいろあるんだが」
rows.en: “Well, there are all kinds of things...”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Of course, there's a lots and a lots, but..."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says simply that there are various things. The English invents repetition and twice combines the singular article with a plural noun.

highlights.text: there's a lots and a lots

rows.jp: 「じゃあ一個だけ質問に答えてあげる。どんなことでも答えるよ？」
rows.en: “Then I'll answer one question. Ask me anything.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Theeen one single solitary question I'll give you an answer to. Ask me anything and I'll answer, OK?"
Taichi: "Co-, color of your panties?"

rows.jp: 「今日は白。でもちょっとかわいいの。ブラとおそろいのやつなんだ」
rows.en: “White today. A cute pair, though. They match my bra.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Today they're white. But they're reeeally cute tho. They totally match the bra!"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the underwear is somewhat cute and matches the bra. The English raises 'somewhat' to 'really' and adds emphatic slang to both clauses.

highlights.text: reeeally cute tho
totally match

ghs.en: Taichi: "Pure whiiite..."

rows.jp: 少女の下着に思いを馳せた。
rows.en: My mind wanders to a young girl's underwear.

ghs.en: I reflect nostalgically on the girl's underwear.
ghs.assessment: 思いを馳せる means letting one's thoughts dwell on something. The English adds nostalgia, which the Japanese does not state.

highlights.text: reflect nostalgically

rows.jp: 「じゃ質問はこれで打ち切ります」
rows.en: “And that's the end of question time.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Well, the questioning round is with this brought to a close."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese straightforwardly closes the questions. The English follows Japanese constituent order into an ungrammatical passive construction.

highlights.text: the questioning round is with this brought to a close

rows.jp: 「うおー、しまったー、世界の謎がー！」
rows.en: “Aargh, I blew it! The mysteries of the world!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Woooooh, dammiiiit, what about the mystery of this wooorld!!!"

rows.jp: 反射的に質問してしまったぁ！

ghs.en: I fired off a question by refleeex!
Taichi: "I am so stupiiid!"
Nanaka: "Also perverted."

Nanaka: "Nooo-ooope."

ghs.en: Nanaka crosses her arm into a X, making the Batten mark of denial and failure.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Nanaka makes an X with her arms. The English retains batten as an unexplained capitalized Japanese word and invents an explanatory doctrine of denial and failure.

highlights.text: the Batten mark of denial and failure

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Next chance, 'K."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says only that there will be another chance. The English appends an unsupported fragment.

highlights.text: had a sharp thought

rows.jp: あれ、こいつ……犯人なんじゃないか。

ghs.en: My my, this one... couldn't she be the culprit?
ghs.assessment: あれ marks sudden realization, like 'wait.' 'My my' is a coy or patronizing exclamation with a different voice.

highlights.text: My my

ghs.en: Taichi: "Nanaka-san... I do have one question..."

rows.jp: 「もうダメだって言ったでしょ」

ghs.en: Nanaka: "I told you that any more are not happening!"
ghs.assessment: Nanaka says she already told him there would be no more questions. The English leaves the plural quantifier without a noun and uses a malformed event predicate.

highlights.text: any more are not happening

ghs.en: Taichi: "Ah, right."

rows.jp: 「また来週だね。太一がちゃんとやることやったら、たどりつくって」
rows.en: “Next week. If you do what you're supposed to, Taichi, you'll get there.”

Taichi: "Manage to get where?"
Nanaka: "This way."
ghs.assessment: ここに answers 'where?' with 'here.' 'This way' instead points out a direction or method.

highlights.text: This way.

ghs.en: Smiling.
Taichi: "Hmmmmmmm."

rows.en: She definitely seems like a key player... but none of this is making any sense.

ghs.assessment: 要領を得ない means that Taichi cannot get a clear answer or make sense of her. It does not mean that she is irrelevant; the preceding clause explicitly calls her a key person.

highlights.text: she doesn't seem to be relevant

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Did you go to the hokora then?
ghs.assessment: 祠 is a small shrine and should not remain as unexplained 'hokora'; the English dialogue also lacks its closing quotation mark.

highlights.text: Nanaka: "Did you go to the hokora then?

ghs.en: Taichi: "I went."

rows.en: “...But you didn't look inside, did you?”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "...you didn't look inside, right?"
Taichi: "I didn't look, now that you remind me."
Nanaka: "Go look."

rows.jp: 「いや、もうあの場所には行きたくないから」
rows.en: “No. I don't want to go back there.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Nah, I just don't really want to go that place anymore."
ghs.assessment: English requires the directional preposition: 'go to that place.'

highlights.text: go that place

rows.jp: 「……ま、焦る必要はないから構わないんだけど」
rows.en: “...Well, there's no need to rush, so that's fine.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "...well, there's no need to really hurry so it doesn't matter, but..."

rows.en: “It's where Yoko sleeps. I want to leave her in peace.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "That's the place where Youko-chan sleeps, so I don't really want to go barging in there."

ghs.en: Nanak: "Hmmm. But that girl, I think, would have wanted you to go there!"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says she thinks the girl would want Taichi to come. The English changes present hypothetical desire to past desire, reverses 'come' to 'go there,' and misspells the speaker name.

highlights.text: Nanak: "Hmmm. But that girl, I think, would have wanted you to go there!"

ghs.en: ...does she know of her death as well?
Taichi: "I'm so ashamed that I can't even look at her face."

rows.jp: 曜子ちゃんの敵討ちをしてやれない俺だ。

ghs.en: Not when I am someone who isn't exacting revenge for you, Youko-chan.
ghs.assessment: Taichi describes himself as someone unable to avenge her, which is why he cannot face her. The English becomes a fragment, directly addresses her with 'you,' and fails to state the relation to the preceding shame.

highlights.text: Not when I am someone who isn't exacting revenge for you, Youko-chan.

rows.en: “That might be a cruel way to think.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "That may be a cruel thought."
Taichi: "How come?"

rows.jp: 「対等でないと合わせる顔がないってことでしょ？」
rows.en: “You mean you can't face her unless the two of you are equals, right?”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "You're saying you're too ashamed to even look at her face because you're not equal, don't you see?"

rows.jp: 「裏返せば、相手にも自分と対等になって欲しいってことだ」
rows.en: “Look at it the other way around, and you're asking her to be your equal.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "If you look it from the opposite side, it's wanting the other side to become equal to yourself, that's what."
ghs.assessment: 裏返せば means 'conversely' or 'looked at the other way.' The English construction lacks the required preposition after 'look' and literalizes a side.

highlights.text: If you look it from the opposite side

ghs.en: Taichi: "Ah... right."
I recognize the inconsistency.

rows.jp: 「ピーナッツ入り柿の種の尊厳を認めるんなら、弱い相手を弱いまま認めないとオカシイんじゃないかな」
rows.en: “If you acknowledge the dignity of peanuts in Kaki no Tane, wouldn't it be strange not to accept a weaker person as weak?”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "If you can accept that there's dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon, then not accepting a weak companion that stays weak is kinda odd isn't it."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese invokes the dignity of the peanuts included in the snack called kaki no tane. The English instead claims that peanuts themselves are referred to as persimmon seeds.

highlights.text: dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon

rows.en: “Yeah. Though Sakuraba is the Kaki no Tane.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Ain't it. Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho."
ghs.assessment: Taichi agrees, then notes that 'kaki no tane' refers to Sakuraba in their analogy. 'Ain't it' reverses agreement, and the English leaves the snack name untranslated inside a malformed possessive fragment.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Ain't it. Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho."

rows.jp: 俺の過去まで知ってやがる。

ghs.en: She seems to even have knowledge of my past.
Anything goes when it comes to her doesn't it...

rows.jp: 「じゃ、気が向いたら行ってみようかな」
rows.en: “Maybe I'll go if the mood strikes me.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Well, if my mind changes I'll maybe give a try and go."
ghs.assessment: 気が向いたら means 'if I feel like it.' The English substitutes a change of mind and omits the object required by 'give a try.'

highlights.text: if my mind changes I'll maybe give a try and go

ghs.en: Nanaka: "'K!"
ghs.assessment: うむ is an affirmative 'yes' or 'mm-hm.' The clipped slang spelling and exclamation are unsupported.

rows.jp: 「あたしもね、人間関係に資格なんてないと思ってる」
rows.en: “You know, I don't think relationships require qualifications.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Me too, yannow, I don't think I'm qualified for human relationships."
ghs.assessment: Nanaka says that human relationships do not require qualifications. The English instead says that she personally lacks the qualifications for any relationship.

highlights.text: I don't think I'm qualified for human relationships

rows.jp: 「太一も一緒の考えなら、嬉しい」
rows.en: “I'd be happy if you thought the same, Taichi.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "The thought that Taichi is the same... it makes me happy."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says she is happy if Taichi shares her view. The English says vaguely that Taichi himself is 'the same.'

highlights.text: The thought that Taichi is the same

ghs.en: Taichi: "......"
Dammit, so cute...

rows.jp: 「部活も頑張れ。仲間が死んでも頑張れ。大丈夫、来週には笑っていられっから」
rows.en: “Work hard at your club. Keep at it even if your friends die. It'll be fine—you'll be laughing next week.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Give it all on club, too. True Companions may die, but still give it all. You'll be all right, because next week you'll be all laughs."
ghs.assessment: Nanaka urges him to persist with the club even if companions die and says he will be able to smile next week. The English turns the concessive event into a possibility, invents a capitalized class, and changes smiling into being an object of laughter.

highlights.text: True Companions may die
you'll be all laughs

rows.jp: 「うわ、不謹慎なこと言うなっ」

ghs.en: Taichi: "Whoa, don't say imprudent stuff!"
ghs.assessment: 不謹慎 means insensitive or inappropriate toward a grave subject. 'Imprudent' means merely unwise or incautious.

highlights.text: imprudent

ghs.en: Taichi: "We got two dead dammiiit!"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that two people are dead. The English turns 'dead' into an unheaded count noun, uses a possession construction, and adds a curse.

highlights.text: We got two dead dammiiit!

rows.jp: 「あー、一応言っとくとあたしが殺したんじゃないよ？」
rows.en: “Ah, I should probably mention that I'm not the one who killed them.”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "Ahhh, just in case, I'ma telling you that I didn't kill them, right?"

rows.jp: 「えーーーーーーーーーーーっ！？」

ghs.en: Taichi: "EHHHHHHHHHHHH?!"

rows.jp: 「……あたしが殺したと確信していたね、キミ？」
rows.en: “...You were convinced I killed them, weren't you?”

ghs.en: Nanaka: "...you were sure I had killed them, weren't ya?"

rows.jp: 「なんかさ、不思議な力持ってそうだし、アリバイとかトリックとか超越して自由に殺せるんじゃないの？　神殺人事件とか言ってさ。推理小説でも何でもないけど」
rows.en: “I mean, you seem to have some mysterious power. Couldn't you kill anyone you wanted, completely beyond alibis or tricks? Call it the God Murder Case. It wouldn't be a detective novel anymore, though.”

ghs.en: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."
ghs.assessment: The English dialogue is missing its opening quotation mark, duplicates 'you,' and renders 自由に殺せる as being 'free' or permitted to murder rather than able to kill without ordinary constraints.

highlights.text: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."

rows.jp: 「うーん、神ってのは近いかもね、けっこう」

ghs.assessment: 神 is generic here and does not require capitalized 'God.' The appended coordination 'and very much so' is also ungrammatical for けっこう, which modifies how close the comparison is.

highlights.text: God might be close I guess, and very much so

rows.jp: 「とか言ってるうちに俺の家だ」
rows.en: “And while we're talking, here we are at my house.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "And while we're talking whatever, here's my house."

ghs.assessment: ひもパン means string panties, not jams.
